cim: Why SAP’s second 10,000-job overhaul in two years matters to CIOs
cim_eredeti: Why SAP’s second 10,000-job overhaul in two years matters to CIOs
szoveg_eredeti:
When SAP restructured roughly 10,000 roles in 2024, executives framed the move as a workforce transformation designed to prepare the company for cloud computing and AI. Two years later, SAP is reportedly considering eliminating another 10,000 positions, but this time the rationale appears different.

Rather than reshaping skills while maintaining headcount, analysts say the latest overhaul reflects a growing belief among technology companies that AI can permanently reduce labor needs, raising new questions for CIOs about vendor stability, support quality, and the economics of the AI era.

The layoffs are expected to impact several departments, including product and engineering, according to a Bloomberg article that reported on the new round of layoffs.

While the 2024 restructuring did not reduce the headcount and was shown as a reshuffle of skills to align with the company’s AI-first strategy, the new round of layoffs appears to be focused on cost reduction and is likely to shrink the company’s employee count by about 9%.

“SAP’s 2024 programme changed who worked there, and this one is about how many,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Grehound Research.

When SAP announced a major restructuring in 2024 affecting roughly 10,000 positions, executives described it as a strategic shift toward cloud computing and AI. The company took a restructuring charge of about €3 billion and repositioned talent toward growth areas, including AI.

SAP did not directly comment on the Bloomberg story, saying it does not comment on speculation. A company spokesperson, however, said, “The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful. As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures.”

For CIOs, the key issue is not the scale of the cuts. It is why a company that already undertook a major restructuring just two years ago believes another overhaul may be necessary.

“AI can reduce manpower requirements in software development, testing, documentation, customer support, pre-sales, and implementation activities. But Tech CEOs were arguing that, because of Jevons Paradox, AI will create more demand for software. In reality, that has not happened yet. CEOs who were saying AI will create more tech jobs are doing layoffs,” said Pareekh Jain, CEO at Pareekh Consulting.

Yet, SAP’s move toward this second restructuring is hardly a surprise, according to analysts.

Gogia describes the move as part of a three-step change at SAP. “First came the slow tightening: Klein’s 2025 talk of one or two per cent a year, then the July 2026 memo focusing new hiring on ‘mainly core AI roles.’ Next came the substitution, which Klein described plainly when he said SAP is balancing token consumption against headcount. Last came the declaration, when Asam told investors the episode of rising headcount was over and spoke of five-digit numbers of employees to be touched.”

Read in sequence, the Bloomberg report is less a surprise than the third step arriving on schedule, with tokens now the fuel the engine prefers to salaries, Gogia added.

SAP avoided using terms such as layoffs or job cuts in its 2024 restructuring plan, terming the changes voluntary programs and internal retraining measures. At the same time, the company has also been unusually vocal about its internal AI gains.

“The autonomous enterprise SAP launched in May 2026 needs data scientists, agent builders and people who understand business processes deeply enough to teach software to run them. Nothing in that roadmap requires a cut of at least 10,000,” Gogia said.

The CIOs who sat through the 2024 reshuffle have reason to feel uneasy, because the first round tested their patience and this one tests their support desk. SAP’s board should publish where the cuts land, function by function, before the January results, said Gogia. CIOs should ask SAP, in writing and before any 2027 renewal, which of their service commitments depend on teams named in the programme, and what SAP will measure to prove service holds.”

Varun has been covering enterprise IT for over two decades, from on-the-ground reports on technology use in remote parts of India to interviews with CEOs of some of the world’s largest companies. He now manages a team of news reporters across the Asia-Pacific region contributing to Foundry’s B-to-B titles: CIO, Computerworld, CSO, InfoWorld, and Network World. He has a Master’s degree in Computer Applications and co-authored the book “Customer First: A mindset that spells success in today’s world.”
